{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}(18z^{2}-26)\,\text{d}V,

question.:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{3{x}^{2}+24}$ at the point where $x=-2.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

We use the chain rule in the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=3{x}^{2}+24.$ Then $y=\sqrt{u}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6x.
$$

Multiplying the two together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}}\cdot 6x \\  & =\frac{3x}{\sqrt{3{x}^{2}+24}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting  $x=-2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=-2} & ={\left(\frac{3x}{\sqrt{3{x}^{2}+24}}\right)|}_{x=-2} \\  & =\frac{(-6)}{\sqrt{3(-2)^{2}+24}} \\  & =-\frac{6}{6} \\  & =-1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $g(x)=x-{x}^{2}$ and $f(g(x))=-\frac{4}{\sqrt{g}}=-4{g}^{-1/2}.$ 

Differentiating, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(g(x)) & =-4({g}^{-1/2})^{′}=4\cdot \frac{1}{2}{g}^{-3/2}=\frac{2}{{g}^{3/2}}, \\ {g}^{′}(x) & =(x-{x}^{2})^{′}=1-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the chain rule, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={f}^{′}(g(x))\cdot {g}^{′}(x) \\  & =\frac{2}{{g}^{3/2}}\cdot (1-2x) \\  & =\frac{2-4x}{\sqrt{(x-{x}^{2})^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](images/5d/5d8a94cd0df8095c78aec955c3d0f062e38410326399104644b24e981eb1db9a.png)

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $4$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=0,$ and

- bounded above by $z=10-x-y=10-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta ,z)\,:\,0\le r\le 4,\,0\le \theta <2\pi ,\,0\le z\le 10-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{10-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }r\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{4}r[z]_{z=0}^{z=10-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{4}r(10-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}10r-{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[5{r}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}{r}^{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )]}_{r=0}^{r=4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }5(4)^{2}-\frac{1}{3}(4)^{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }80-\frac{64}{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={[80\theta -\frac{64}{3}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )]}_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi } \\  & =80(2\pi -0)-\frac{64}{3}(0-1-0+1) \\  & =160\pi .\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨3x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,{x}^{7}+y⟩
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/00/00bceda1bdf4f515646b3a1e8476f1eadde721aa52dbc9be9c7e866bcab99d3b.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=3x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{7}+y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=3,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le {x}^{5}\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{5}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\,{|}_{0}^{{x}^{5}}\,dx \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{5}\,dx \\  & =4\left(\frac{{x}^{6}}{6}\right){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}-0 \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
